a1.say: Let's solve The One Repeated Number, using the Fast and Slow Pointers approach.

a1.cap: nums has n + 1 integers, each between 1 and n, so at least one value repeats. Exactly one value is repeated (possibly many times). Return it without modifying nums and using only O(1) extra memory.
a1.say: nums has n plus 1 integers, each between 1 and n, so at least one value repeats. Exactly one value is repeated (possibly many times). Return it without modifying nums and using only O of one extra memory.

lines: nums has n + 1 integers, each between 1 and n, so at least one value repeats. Exactly one value is repeated (possibly many times). Return it without modifying nums and using only O(1) extra memory.

a1.cap: For example, with nums = [1,3,4,2,2], the answer is 2.
a1.say: For example, with nums equals 1, 3, 4, 2, 2, the answer is 2.

a1.cap: Treat each value as an arrow to an index. Because two positions hold the same value, two arrows point at the same index, which creates a cycle whose entrance is the duplicate.
Move a slow pointer one hop and a fast pointer two hops until they meet. Then restart slow from the beginning and move both one hop at a time: they meet exactly at the duplicate.
Let's walk through it with nums = [1,3,4,2,2].
a1.say: Let's walk through it with nums equals 1, 3, 4, 2, 2.

a1.cap: Slow hops to 3; fast hops twice to 2.
Slow hops to 2; fast hops twice to 2.
They met inside the cycle. Restart slow from the beginning.
Both hop once: slow is 3, fast is 4.
Both hop once: slow is 2, fast is 2.
Time complexity is O(n) and extra space is O(1). Floyd's cycle detection takes linear time and just two variables.
a1.say: Time complexity is O of n and extra space is O of one. Floyd's cycle detection takes linear time and just two variables.

a1.cap: That's the Fast & Slow Pointers approach. Now try writing it yourself, in Java or Python!
